1.text:
How Can Moons Far From the Sun Stay So Warm?

Out past Mars, the Sun shrinks to a bright dot and its warmth fades fast. You might expect the outer solar system to be frozen and dead. It isn't, and figuring out why is the point of this deck.

In this deck we visit the four giant planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, along with their rings and moons. Some of those moons are among the most active worlds anywhere. One has hundreds of volcanoes. Several hide oceans of liquid water under their ice. One has rain, rivers, and seas, but not of water. And one shoots out geysers.

Sunlight out there is far too weak to explain any of that. So where does the energy come from? That's the question you'll be able to answer by the end. To warm up, take one minute and write down one thing you think is true about Jupiter.

Did you know? The four little planets along the bottom of this page are drawn roughly to scale with each other. Can you tell which is which?

2.text:
Today I Can...

Here's the plan for this deck. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements so you can check yourself at the end.

I can describe what gas giants and ice giants are made of, inside and out. I can explain why Saturn's density is lower than water's. I can explain belts, zones, and the Great Red Spot. I can explain what makes a giant planet's magnetosphere. I can describe rings and explain the Roche limit. I can use orbital periods to show the 1 : 2 : 4 resonance. I can describe Io, Europa, Ganymede, Titan, Enceladus, and Triton. And I can compare Titan's methane cycle and Io's volcanoes with Earth.

That's eight goals, each tagged with an Indiana standard or marked as enrichment. Rate yourself 1 to 3 on each now, and again at the end.

3.text:
Meet the Jovian Planets

A Jovian planet is a giant planet made of hydrogen, helium, and hydrogen compounds, with no solid surface. There's nowhere to land. The air just gets thicker and hotter the deeper you go.

Here they are, drawn to scale next to Earth. Jupiter is 142,984 km across, and Saturn is 120,536 km. These two are the gas giants, made mostly of hydrogen and helium, like the Sun. Uranus (51,118 km) and Neptune (49,528 km) are smaller. They're the ice giants, and most of their mass is hydrogen compounds like water, ammonia, and methane.

Now find Earth on the slide, at 12,756 km. Tiny, right? Picture Earth as a 1 cm bead. Then Jupiter would be about 11 cm across, about the size of a grapefruit.

Did you know? All four giants have rings, lots of moons, and magnetic fields, and they all spin faster than Earth.

4.text:
Inside a Gas Giant

Let's ride an imaginary elevator down into Jupiter. At the top are the cloud tops, made of hydrogen (H₂) and helium (He) gas. As you sink deeper, the pressure and temperature climb, and the gas slowly turns into liquid hydrogen. There's no sharp line where gas becomes liquid.

Go deeper still, and the pressure gets so extreme that hydrogen turns into metallic hydrogen: hydrogen squeezed so hard that it conducts electricity like a metal. It's still a liquid, though, not a solid like iron.

At the very center, scientists used to picture a small, solid core. But NASA's Juno spacecraft found clues that the core is big and "fuzzy," partly dissolved into the hydrogen around it. Saturn has the same layers, just with less metallic hydrogen because it has less mass.

Did you know? NASA calls Jupiter's liquid hydrogen "the largest ocean in the solar system," made of hydrogen instead of water.

5.text:
Inside an Ice Giant

Uranus and Neptune have a different recipe. About 80% of their mass is hot, dense "ices": water, ammonia (NH₃), and methane (CH₄). They're called ices because they were frozen grains back when the planets formed. Inside the planets now, they're a hot fluid, not frozen at all.

Look at the Neptune cutaway. At the center is a small rocky core. Around it is the thick layer of fluid water, ammonia, and methane. On top is an atmosphere of hydrogen, helium, and a little methane.

That methane is what gives these planets their blue-green color. It soaks up red light and reflects blue. Uranus and Neptune formed farther out, where planets grew slowly, so they grabbed much less gas before the young Sun blew it away.

Did you know? Near the core of Uranus, the temperature may reach about 4,982 °C (9,000 °F).

6.text:
Diamond Rain?

Here's one of the stranger ideas in planetary science. Remember, it's a hypothesis, not something anyone has seen.

Deep inside Uranus and Neptune, the pressure is crushing. It might be strong enough to strip the hydrogen right off methane molecules. That would leave the carbon behind, and the carbon could get squeezed into diamonds that sink down toward the core.

That's why there's a question mark in the title. Lab experiments suggest it's possible, but we haven't been there to watch it happen.

7.text:
Saturn Would Float

Density is how much mass is packed into a space. Saturn's average density is 687 kg/m³. Water's is 1,000 kg/m³. That makes Saturn the only planet less dense than water!

NASA likes to say Saturn could float in a bathtub, if anyone could find a bathtub big enough. The reason is Saturn's recipe. It's made mostly of hydrogen and helium, the two lightest elements, and it doesn't have as much mass as Jupiter to squeeze them tight.

Saturn's low density and fast spin, about 10.5 hours, also make it the most squashed planet. Its middle bulges about 10% wider than it is from pole to pole.

Did you know? Saturn isn't actually light. It has 95 times Earth's mass. It's just spread out over a huge volume.

8.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Time to check Part 1. Why is Saturn less dense than water?

Is it because A) it's made mostly of the lightest elements, H and He, B) it's hollow inside, C) its rings hold it up, or D) it's made of frozen water ice?

Look back at Slides 4, 5, and 7, pick your answer, and be ready to explain why the others don't work.

9.text:
Belts and Zones

Jupiter's colorful stripes are cloud bands. Banding means bright zones of rising air and dark belts of sinking air, all wrapped around the planet. In the zones, rising air builds high, bright clouds. In the belts, sinking air lets us see down to deeper, darker clouds.

Jupiter spins once in about 10 hours, which is fast for something that size. That fast spin stretches the rising and sinking air into long bands that wrap all the way around. Powerful jet streams blow east and west in turn between them.

The winds are strong: about 150 m/s on Jupiter and about 500 m/s on Saturn. Neptune's winds top 2,000 km per hour, the fastest in the solar system.

Did you know? Neptune gets only about 1/900 of the sunlight Earth does, yet it has the fastest winds. Much of a giant planet's weather is powered by heat from inside.

10.text:
The Great Red Spot

The Great Red Spot is a giant storm on Jupiter, about 1.3 times as wide as Earth. Look at Earth drawn at the same scale on the slide. Our whole planet could fit inside it! It's been tracked since 1831, so it's been churning for more than 190 years.

It spins counterclockwise, and it's deep. When NASA's Juno spacecraft flew over it, its measurements showed the storm reaches about 500 km below the cloud tops.

Why does it last so long? On Earth, a hurricane dies when it moves over land. Jupiter has no land to slow a storm down, so the Great Red Spot just keeps going. It is slowly shrinking, though.

Did you know? Neptune had its own Great Dark Spot when Voyager 2 flew past in 1989. Later, it vanished.

11.text:
Magnetic Bubbles

A magnetosphere is the bubble of space controlled by a planet's magnetic field. All four giants have one. Jupiter's field comes from that spinning layer of liquid metallic hydrogen deep inside, and it's about 15 times stronger than Earth's.

Look at the diagram. The solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun, pushes on one side of the bubble and stretches the other side into a long tail. Jupiter's magnetotail reaches all the way past Saturn's orbit! That makes Jupiter's magnetosphere one of the biggest things in the solar system. (The drawing isn't to scale.)

Inside the bubble, charged particles create intense radiation belts and bright auroras near Jupiter's poles. Spacecraft that visit need shielding to protect their electronics.

Did you know? Volcanic gases from Jupiter's moon Io help fill a doughnut-shaped cloud of charged particles around the planet.

12.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Let's check Part 2. What makes Jupiter's strong magnetic field?

Is it A) spinning liquid metallic hydrogen deep inside, B) a giant iron bar magnet at its center, C) the swirling Great Red Spot, or D) the solar wind blowing past it?

Look back at Slides 4 and 11. Choose one, and be ready to explain why the other three don't fit.

13.text:
All Four Giants Have Rings

A planetary ring is made of countless pieces of ice, rock, or dust, each orbiting the planet like a tiny moon. Rings aren't solid sheets, and Saturn isn't the only planet that has them. All four giants have rings, and they're all different.

Jupiter's rings are thin and dark, made of dust. Saturn's are the bright superstars, made of ice in pieces from dust grains up to the size of a house. Uranus has 13 narrow, dark rings, and since the planet is tipped 98°, its rings are tipped too. Neptune has 5 rings plus some clumpy arcs.

Saturn's rings are absurdly thin for their size. They reach out hundreds of thousands of kilometers from the planet, but the main rings are often only about 10 m thick.

Did you know? Saturn's rings look so bright because ice reflects sunlight. Dark dust soaks it up, which is why Jupiter's rings are so faint.

14.text:
The Roche Limit

You learned that a moon pulls harder on Earth's near side than its far side, which makes tides. A planet does the same thing to its moons. Far from the planet, a moon's own gravity easily holds it together.

But get too close, and the stretch gets stronger than the moon's own gravity. The Roche limit is the distance inside which a planet's tides tear a moon apart. Look at the slide. Inside the line, a moon is stretched and torn into ring pieces. Outside it, pieces can clump together into a moon.

That's why the main rings of all four giants sit close to their planets, inside the Roche limit, while the big moons orbit farther out. Saturn's rings may be pieces of comets, asteroids, or moons that broke up.

Did you know? The Roche limit is named after the French astronomer Édouard Roche, who worked it out in 1848.

15.text:
Phobos Is Falling

Mars has a small moon named Phobos, and it's in trouble. Phobos is slowly spiraling inward, getting closer to Mars over time.

Here's why. Mars spins slower than Phobos orbits it. So the tidal bulge Phobos raises on Mars lags behind, and it keeps tugging Phobos backward, shrinking its orbit bit by bit.

Follow the picture to "later." Scientists predict that in roughly 30 to 50 million years, Phobos will cross the Roche limit and Mars's tides will tear it apart into a ring. It might crash into Mars instead.

16.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 3

Time to sort. For each card, decide: is it inside or outside the Roche limit?

A) Saturn's main rings. B) Titan. C) A moon that drifts too close. D) The Galilean moons.

Put each card in the INSIDE box (torn into rings) or the OUTSIDE box (moons can survive). Use the words "tides" and "own gravity" to explain each choice.

17.text:
Tidal Heating

Here's what keeps the most active moons busy. Tidal heating is heat made when a planet's tides squeeze and flex a moon over and over.

Io orbits very close to Jupiter, on a slightly oval path (exaggerated on the slide). When Io swings closer, Jupiter stretches it more. When it swings farther away, Jupiter stretches it less. So Io gets squeezed and relaxed again and again, every 1.77 days. All that flexing heats up its insides. It's like bending a paper clip back and forth until it gets warm.

Why doesn't Io's orbit settle into a perfect circle? Its neighbors Europa and Ganymede give it small, well-timed tugs that keep it oval. That's on the next page.

Did you know? In 1979, scientists used this idea to predict Io would have volcanoes. Days later, Voyager 1 photographed them erupting.

18.text:
A Clockwork of Moons

Three of Jupiter's moons move like gears in a clock. Io takes 1.77 days to orbit Jupiter. Europa takes 3.55 days. Ganymede takes 7.15 days. Notice anything? Each period is about double the one before it.

That's a 1 : 2 : 4 resonance. In the time Ganymede orbits once, Europa orbits twice and Io four times. So they line up again and again in the same spots. Their small gravity tugs on each other always push the same way instead of canceling out, and that keeps Io's and Europa's orbits slightly oval. That keeps the tidal heating going.

Kepler's third law from Deck 3 explains the spacing: moons farther out take longer to orbit. (The drawing isn't to scale.)

Did you know? Jupiter's fourth big moon, Callisto, isn't part of the resonance. It's barely heated, and its old surface is packed with craters.

19.text:
Volcanoes: Io vs Earth

Io is the most volcanically active world in the solar system. It's only a little bigger than our Moon, but it has hundreds of volcanoes. Some blast plumes tall enough for the Hubble Space Telescope to photograph from Earth orbit. Io's surface gets repaved so often that it has almost no impact craters.

Compare the two sides of the slide. Both Io and Earth have volcanoes, made when melted rock reaches the surface. The difference is the energy source. Io is heated by tides from Jupiter. Earth is heated from inside, by leftover heat and radioactive decay, and its magma comes from radioactive heat and plate motion.

Here's a good sign that tides matter. Our Moon is about the same size as Io, and it went quiet billions of years ago. Io's volcanoes can't be running on leftover heat alone.

Did you know? Io's bright yellow and orange colors probably come from sulfur compounds.

20.text:
Hidden Oceans

Europa is covered in a smooth, cracked shell of ice. Underneath, scientists have strong evidence for a salty ocean sitting on top of rock. Europa's ocean may hold about twice the water of all Earth's oceans combined. Not bad for a moon smaller than our own!

How? Earth's oceans average less than 4 km deep. Europa's ocean is thought to be many tens of kilometers deep and to cover the whole moon. Tidal heating keeps it liquid.

Ganymede has a hidden ocean too, possibly stacked in layers between sheets of ice like a club sandwich. Why do scientists care so much? Liquid water, energy, and the right chemistry are the ingredients for life as we know it. NASA's Europa Clipper spacecraft arrives in 2030 to take a closer look.

Did you know? Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, bigger than the planet Mercury, and it's the only moon known to make its own magnetic field.

21.text:
Check for Understanding: Do the Math

Time to prove the clockwork yourself. Here are the orbital periods: Io 1.77 days, Europa 3.55 days, and Ganymede 7.15 days.

Step 1: divide the periods to show the 1 : 2 : 4 pattern. Step 2: draw 4 Io laps, and show where Europa and Ganymede are during that time. Step 3: explain how the moons' tugs keep the tidal heating going.

22.text:
Enceladus's Plumes

Enceladus is a small, icy moon of Saturn, only about 500 km across. But in the 2000s, the Cassini spacecraft spotted something odd. Plumes of water vapor and ice grains were spraying out of long cracks near its south pole, nicknamed the "tiger stripes."

A plume is a jet of water vapor and ice grains sprayed out from an ocean under the ice. Look at the cut-open south pole on the slide. Under the ice shell is a global salty ocean, and under that is a rocky core. There may even be warm vents on the seafloor, like the ones on Earth's ocean floor.

The spray spreads out along Enceladus's orbit and feeds Saturn's E ring. When Cassini flew through the plumes, it found water, salts, and organic molecules. (The drawing isn't to scale.)

Did you know? In 2017, NASA deliberately plunged Cassini into Saturn so it could never crash into Enceladus and contaminate it.

23.text:
Titan's Methane Cycle

Titan, Saturn's biggest moon, is the only moon with a thick atmosphere, made mostly of nitrogen, like Earth's. It's also the only world besides Earth known to have lakes and seas on its surface. But Titan is so cold that water is rock-hard ice. Its liquids are methane (CH₄) and ethane.

That gives Titan a methane cycle: Titan's version of the water cycle. Compare the two sides of the slide. On Titan, clouds drop methane rain, it flows into methane lakes and seas, and then it evaporates back into the sky. On Earth, clouds drop rain and snow, it flows into oceans and lakes, and then it evaporates. Same steps, different liquid.

The surface even has river channels and shorelines, carved by the methane cycle, much like water shapes Earth.

Did you know? NASA's Dragonfly, a flying drone, is scheduled to launch to Titan in 2028.

24.text:
3 Ways to Get a Moon

How did a moon come to be? Its orbit is a clue. There are three main ways a planet gets a moon.

One: it formed in a disk around the planet. These moons have round orbits and go the same direction the planet spins. Jupiter's big moons formed this way. Two: an impact. A giant crash throws out a ring of debris that gathers into a moon, like ours. Three: it was captured. A passing object gets grabbed by the planet's gravity. These moons have tilted, stretched orbits, and they may even go backward. Jupiter's small, far-out moons were captured.

So when you meet a new moon, ask three questions. Does it go the same direction? Is its orbit round? Does it orbit along the planet's equator?

25.text:
Triton Goes Backward

Meet Triton, Neptune's largest moon. It's the only large moon in the solar system with a retrograde orbit: an orbit that runs opposite to the planet's spin. Look at the arrows on the slide. Neptune spins one way, and Triton orbits the other way.

That's a big clue. Moons that form in a disk around a planet orbit the same way the planet spins. So Triton probably didn't form around Neptune. Scientists think it was captured from the Kuiper Belt. It's similar to Pluto in size and what it's made of. (The drawing isn't to scale.)

Triton is far from dead, too. When Voyager 2 flew past in 1989, it found active geysers.

Did you know? Neptune's tides are slowly shrinking Triton's orbit. Far in the future, it may cross the Roche limit and become a ring.

26.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 5

Here's the last check. Which clue best shows Triton was captured?

Is it A) it orbits opposite to Neptune's spin, B) it has a thin nitrogen atmosphere, C) it's covered in frozen nitrogen, or D) it's the largest moon of Neptune?

Careful: more than one of these is true. The question is which one is the best evidence. Look back at Slide 24 before you choose.

27.text:
Exit Ticket

You just toured the whole outer solar system. Show what you've got with three quick questions.

First, name one way a gas giant differs from an ice giant inside. Second, how can a moon far from the Sun have volcanoes or an ocean? Third, give one way Titan's methane cycle is like Earth's water cycle, and one way it's different.

When you're done, look at the Jupiter fact you wrote on Slide 1. Would you change it? Then rate yourself 1 to 3 on each "I can" statement from Slide 2.

29.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask you to do, in plain words.

ES.2.2: describe the different kinds of objects in the solar system, including planets, moons, comets, asteroids, and protoplanets. Know that planets have been found orbiting other stars, and even drifting with no star at all. And describe how our solar system is organized, from the rocky and giant planets to the asteroid belt and the Oort Cloud.

ES.2.4: use math or computer models to show how planets, moons, comets, and asteroids move, and explain that Kepler's laws come straight from Newton's law of gravity and his laws of motion. Your ES.2.4 task in this deck is the resonance math on Slide 21.
